root_draft.speaker: agent
root_draft.text: The Webwork is a quiet jungle already owned by something that regards everything in it as food. Walking into its hush feels like trespassing; landing a ship draws an answer. Thick silk cables run through living trees, with sticky threads between them and fine carpet at the spiders' sites. Touching the web or carrying stolen eggs gives its hunters a way to find you. Sunlit clearings and fire give the colony ground to defend, while the growing canopy threatens that refuge. Its treasure makes returning tempting: thrixweave for fine equipment and strong tethers, and inert eggs worth smuggling. Rare traders can resell the silk dearly. A gutter specimen teaches the crewed traction lance, sharing its pull with the Sump's capstan and turning a spider's dependence on shade against it. The wrapped bones of an urraveth show what the owners can consume; reading them earns silk, and loading them risks a collapse that warns first. Beyond the jungle, its spiders can besiege shaded neighbours by visibly spinning their own approach, binding doors and cocooning fallen colonists. The player should learn to read the place and make dangerous trips into it, rather than mistake silence for safety.

asks.text: Where does the proposed root misunderstand that experience, and which moment has to work before you would call this the Webwork?
asks.decision: If trespass leads, organise the core around entry, being noticed and escape. If temptation leads, organise it around the expedition and its cost. If the outward threat leads, lead with the siege and connect it back to its home. Retain coverage of every built capability in all cases. A corrected promise rewrites dependent claims; silence approves nothing.
asks.why: F1/F2. A quiet map with valuable loot could pass the words while missing the sense of ownership and pursuit. Your experience sentence and the ship-versus-foot distinction stand; this asks what the draft has failed to connect.
asks.picture: A small party enters on foot. Almost nothing calls. They find silk worth taking, then realise their way back runs through a place that has noticed them. Later, the same jungle sends spiders toward a neighbouring settlement.

guess.speaker: agent
guess.text: The hush makes the intrusion frightening; taking treasure turns that fear into a decision. I would lead with that cause and consequence.

asks.author: Codex Designer dry run

review.note: Local evidence/wording check only. No fresh author-independent reviewer verdict.

asks.text: Which scene should come first when deciding whether we understood this biome, and what single failure there would make you stop the demonstration?
asks.decision: The selected scene becomes showcase 1 only after your recorded pick. A needs separate acceptance for sound, detection, taking treasure and the resulting pursuit, plus their interaction. B needs natural eligibility and autonomous advance as well as individual siege mechanics. C needs actual examine jobs and a warning/rescue control. The other capabilities still get ordinary scenes or later showcases; root approval alone is not a showcase pick.
asks.why: F1/F2/F3. No flagship pick was found. A room full of spawned objects would demonstrate neither the expedition nor the siege.
asks.picture: Three possible scene cards: A, walk in quietly, take silk or eggs, and get out under pressure; B, defend a shaded neighbour while spiders visibly spin toward the base; C, examine the dead giant, then unload a creaking bone before it falls. The lance gets its own scene whichever comes first.

guess.speaker: agent
guess.text: A first, because it joins the hush, treasure and ownership in ordinary play; B next as a different use of the same owners. I recommend A.

asks.author: Codex Designer dry run

review.note: Local evidence/wording check only. No fresh author-independent reviewer verdict.

asks.text: What should the landing's response make the crew do before unloading, and what happens if they leave immediately?
asks.decision: Immediate pressure needs a close arrival-and-escape scene; an approaching force needs a measured approach and warning. A response that persists after departure needs a saved consequence and a return-visit case. In every answer, contrast the same site entered on foot and preserve the already-ruled guaranteed response to landing.
asks.why: F1. “Always gets a response” is settled; whether that means immediate danger at the hull, an approaching threat, or a mobilisation they can escape has not been pinned down in the evidence read. I found no dedicated landing response to demonstrate.
asks.picture: A ship lands in a cleared patch. Its crew can still leave. Under the canopy nearby, the owners react to the arrival. A second visit by people walking in remains the quiet comparison you already specified.

guess.speaker: agent
guess.text: A readable mobilisation toward the landing, giving the crew a choice to retreat or commit; leaving avoids that encounter without making the landing go unnoticed.

asks.author: Codex Designer dry run

review.note: Local evidence/wording check only. No fresh author-independent reviewer verdict.

asks.text: What chance should a careful party still have after that first thrum, and what mistake should turn it into an ambush they cannot easily escape?
asks.decision: An escape window needs separated hunter distances and a real retreat control. Immediate nearby ambush with distant reinforcement needs separate local and arriving threats. If warning time is deliberately unreliable, require an earlier readable risk that careful play can act on. These answers set the response bar; repairing legacy lookups and building the already-promised consumer remain code work, not new owner decisions.
asks.why: F1/F3. Detection and a sound can exist without meaningful hunting. The sitting already specifies carrier marking and pursuit; the remaining question is the useful decision between notice and capture, not whether the web should notice.
asks.picture: A silk cutter hears the thrum. One hunter is close and another is farther away. The cutter can head for a clearing, tend a bound companion, or try to finish the job. Leaving an egg on the ground ends the carrying condition; it is not permission to erase an existing pursuit.

guess.speaker: agent
guess.text: Reacting promptly should offer an escape toward genuine sunlight; lingering to finish the harvest or crossing farther under canopy should let the hunters close.

asks.author: Codex Designer dry run

review.note: Local evidence/wording check only. No fresh author-independent reviewer verdict.

asks.text: After a successful trip, what should each party be able to make or afford, and what should still tempt them back?
asks.decision: A few exceptional pieces gives a small-party reward scene; colony-wide supply gives a throughput and repeated-trip scene. Eggs as the main payout needs a demonstrated selling route, with campaign outlets proved separately. Silk as the main payoff needs crafting or tether use after extraction. Your picture sets yield, time and risk targets together; it does not reopen inert eggs or rare resale.
asks.why: F2/F3. The current yields and detection chances are engineering defaults, and the terrain/weather item explicitly leaves their balance for your review. A huge haul can empty the reason to return; a tiny haul can make the danger pointless.
asks.picture: A modest colony sends a guarded party for silk and eggs. Later, a forty-colonist settlement sends a much stronger expedition. Both have rare, expensive trader resale as the already-ruled alternative; neither can turn ordinary eggs into farmed spiders.

guess.speaker: agent
guess.text: The small party earns a noticeable equipment improvement or a valuable sale; the large expedition equips several people but still has reasons to return. Rare resale should be a costly fallback.

asks.text: When the neglected margin becomes dangerous, what should an attentive player have noticed in time, and how much of the colony's routine should keeping it safe occupy?
asks.decision: Mostly scheduled labour needs a multi-day work-order scene. Periodic emergencies need an advance sign and a measured response opportunity. Frequent tactical care needs a scene that makes the cost and payoff explicit. If labour quantity does not matter, leave it advisory and keep only the readable loss of protection as core. No answer introduces a new kind of heat or silently turns scald lethal.
asks.why: F1/F3. A clearing can be meaningful defence, a trivial permanent exploit, or exhausting maintenance. Those are different colony experiences even with identical sun-scald code. The existing geometry and scald rulings already settle the physics.
asks.picture: A forty-colonist base has a maintained sunlit margin. Someone allows the canopy to grow back across one approach while outdoor workers carry on elsewhere. The owners' sun-scald must still obey “cripple, never down”; an electric lamp does not replace the sun.

guess.speaker: agent
guess.text: Readable canopy recovery and a useful work commitment, with occasional urgent intervention; routine upkeep should not require individually babysitting forty people.

asks.decision: Physical scale as the payoff needs an in-place recognition scene at play and study zoom. Reconstructing the death needs the player to read evidence across pieces. Excavation tension needs actual work, a warned overloaded case and an unloaded control. Any mix can share one visit but keeps distinct proof for reading and collapse; the four chapters are not put back up for decision.
asks.why: F2/F3. Correct chapter flags and a final letter can pass while the site fails to convey that these spiders consumed something enormous. This asks about the payoff of a built promise, not whether to retain it.

asks.text: What should a well-prepared colony accomplish before the web reaches its doors, and what should still be dangerous after that preparation?
asks.decision: Denying an approach needs paired continuous-shade and interrupted-shade routes. Shooting spinners as the central answer needs interrupted work to prevent silk placement and a readable advance when left alone. Holding the base and rescuing people needs actual door and cocoon jobs during an autonomous attack. Your answer sets pacing and tactical proof, without reopening shaded-only eligibility, the one-day rescue rule or persistent silk.
asks.why: F1/F3. A forced spin job proves one web, not a siege. The unruled pace determines whether preparation matters or whether the event becomes a normal animal rush with decoration.
asks.picture: Spiders begin spinning in trees beyond a neighbouring base. The colony can burn or fell part of their shaded approach, attack the spinners, or prepare a rescue team. A wrapped colonist still gets the already-ruled day before suffocation; the silk stays until dealt with and its harvest stays capped.

guess.speaker: agent
guess.text: Disrupt a shaded approach and force the attackers to spend time finding another useful position, while exposed workers and fallen colonists remain urgent risks.

asks.decision: Ordinary spiders need pack-versus-passer interaction, with the visitor still homed in its own biome. Numbers and coordination put the emphasis on group behaviour rather than another body. A distinct larger creature needs its own scope decision and content; no new queen or caste is inferred. Whichever answer, the already-built remains and ordinary ollathrix stay covered.
asks.why: F1/F2. Your neighbouring-giant battle is recorded in the October 22 Q3 answer, with this exact detail left open. I found neither an authored Webwork passage list nor its battle behaviour. The old unchosen resident giant is not a substitute.

That would need its own content decision; it cannot silently become a queen or caste of the one existing owner kind.

guess.speaker: agent
guess.text: Ordinary elephant-wide ollathrix hunting together. I recommend that reading because it preserves the one-species decision and makes the remains' story happen in front of us.
